claim: Weights in Weighted Round Robin routing can be any number between 0 and 255.
question: What range of weights can a weighted record have?

values.display: between 0 and 255

qualifiers.condition: FAQ statement; check the developer guide for weight 0 behavior

evidence.quote: Weights can be any number between 0 and 255.

claim: Weighted Round Robin assigns weights to record sets to set how often each response is served, for example for A/B testing with a small portion of traffic.
question: What does weighted routing do, and what is one use for it?

values.display: A/B testing

evidence.quote: Weighted Round Robin allows you to assign weights to resource record sets in order to specify the frequency with which different responses are served.
You may want to use this capability to do A/B testing, sending a small portion of traffic to a server on which you’ve made a software change.

claim: With two weighted record sets of weight 3 and weight 1 for one DNS name, the weight 3 record is returned 75% of the time and the weight 1 record 25% of the time.
question: With weights 3 and 1 on two records, how often is each record returned?

values.display: 75% of the time
25% of the time

qualifiers.scope: two weighted records for one DNS name

evidence.quote: In this case, 75% of the time Route 53 will return the record set with weight 3 and 25% of the time Route 53 will return the record set with weight 1.

claim: Latency Based Routing lets you run applications in multiple AWS Regions, and Amazon Route 53 routes end users to the AWS Region that provides the lowest latency.
question: What does latency-based routing do?

values.display: region that provides the lowest latency

evidence.quote: You can run applications in multiple AWS regions and Amazon Route 53, using dozens of edge locations worldwide, will route end users to the AWS region that provides the lowest latency.

claim: Latency Based Routing uses latency measurements between viewer networks and AWS data centers to decide which endpoint to direct users to.
question: What data does latency-based routing use to choose an endpoint?

values.display: latency measurements between viewer networks and AWS datacenters

evidence.quote: LatencyBased Routing utilizes latency measurements between viewer networks and AWS datacenters.
These measurements are used to determine which endpoint to direct users toward.

claim: Geolocation (Geo DNS) routing directs requests to specific endpoints based on the geographic location from which the request originates.
question: What does geolocation (Geo DNS) routing base its decision on?

values.display: geographic location from which the request originates

evidence.quote: Route 53 Geo DNS lets you balance load by directing requests to specific endpoints based on the geographic location from which the request originates.

claim: Geo DNS makes it possible to customize localized content, such as presenting detail pages in the right language, or to restrict distribution of content to only the markets you have licensed.
question: What are two use cases for geolocation routing?

values.display: restricting distribution of content to only the markets you have licensed

evidence.quote: Geo DNS makes it possible to customize localized content, such as presenting detail pages in the right language or restricting distribution of content to only the markets you have licensed.

claim: Geo DNS balances load across endpoints in a predictable way, so each end-user location is consistently routed to the same endpoint.
question: Does geolocation routing send one location to the same endpoint every time?

values.display: consistently routed to the same endpoint

evidence.quote: Geo DNS also lets you balance load across endpoints in a predictable, easy-to-manage way, ensuring that each end-user location is consistently routed to the same endpoint.

claim: Geo DNS provides three levels of geographic granularity (continent, country and state) and a global record that is served when a user's location matches none of the specific records.
question: What levels of geographic granularity does Geo DNS offer, and what is the global record for?

values.display: three levels of geographic granularity

evidence.quote: Geo DNS provides three levels of geographic granularity: continent, country, and state, and Geo DNS also provides a global record which is served in cases where an end user’s location doesn’t match any of the specific Geo DNS records you have created.

claim: AWS strongly recommends a global (default) Geo DNS record so Route 53 can answer queries from all possible locations; it is returned when the IP address is not in the Geo IP database or the location matches no specific record.
question: Do you need a global record with Geo DNS, and when is it returned?

values.display: we strongly recommend that you configure a global record

evidence.quote: Yes, we strongly recommend that you configure a global record, to ensure that Route 53 can provide a response to DNS queries from all possible locations—even if you have created specific records for each continent, country, or state where you expect your end users will be located.
The DNS query comes from an IP address not recognized by Route 53’s Geo IP database.
The DNS query comes from a location not included in any of the specific Geo DNS records you have created.

claim: Geo DNS records can overlap, and Route 53 returns the most specific one: state first, then country, then continent, and finally the global record.
question: In what order does Route 53 pick among overlapping Geo DNS records?

values.display: most specific Geo DNS record

evidence.quote: For each end user’s location, Route 53 will return the most specific Geo DNS record that includes that location.

In other words, for a given end user’s location, Route 53 will first return a state record; if no state record is found, Route 53 will return a country record; if no country record is found, Route 53 will return a continent record; and finally, if no continent record is found, Route 53 will return the global record.

claim: To minimize end-user latency the FAQ recommends Latency Based Routing; for compliance, localization or other cases that need stable routing from a geography to an endpoint, it recommends Geo DNS.
question: When should you pick latency-based routing and when geolocation routing?

values.display: we recommend using Latency Based Routing
we recommend using Geo DNS

evidence.quote: If your goal is to minimize end-user latency, we recommend using Latency Based Routing.
If you have compliance, localization requirements, or other use cases that require stable routing from a specific geography to a specific endpoint, we recommend using Geo DNS.

claim: Geo DNS bases routing decisions on the geographic location of the requests, and in some cases geography is a good proxy for latency but in others it is not.
question: What is the difference between Latency Based Routing and Geo DNS?

values.display: geographic location of the requests

evidence.quote: Geo DNS bases routing decisions on the geographic location of the requests.
In some cases, geography is a good proxy for latency; but there are certainly situations where it is not.

claim: Amazon Route 53 supports up to eight healthy records in response to each DNS query for multivalue answer routing.
question: How many healthy records can a multivalue answer response contain?

values.display: up to eight healthy records

evidence.quote: Amazon Route 53 supports up to eight healthy records in response to each DNS query.

claim: Returning multiple health-checkable IP addresses is not a substitute for a load balancer, but it is a way to use DNS to improve availability and load balancing.
question: Does multivalue answer routing replace a load balancer?

values.display: not a substitute for a load balancer

evidence.quote: While not a substitute for a load balancer, the ability to return multiple health-checkable IP addresses in response to DNS queries is a way to use DNS to improve availability and load balancing.

claim: To route traffic randomly to multiple resources, create one multivalue answer record for each resource and optionally associate a Route 53 health check with each record.
question: How do you set up multivalue answer routing for several web servers?

values.display: one multivalue answer record for each resource

evidence.quote: If you want to route traffic randomly to multiple resources, such as web servers, you can create one multivalue answer record for each resource and, optionally, associate an Amazon Route 53 health check with each record.

claim: You can list multiple IP addresses for one A record, and the service answers DNS requests with the list of all configured IP addresses.
question: Can a single A record hold more than one IP address?

values.display: multiple IP addresses for an A record

evidence.quote: Amazon Route 53 allows you to list multiple IP addresses for an A record and responds to DNS requests with the list of all configured IP addresses.

claim: Traffic Flow is a global traffic management service that connects users to the best endpoint based on latency, geography and endpoint health, using a visual policy builder in the console.
question: What is Route 53 Traffic Flow?

values.display: global traffic management service

evidence.quote: Amazon Route 53 Traffic Flow is an easy-to-use and cost-effective global traffic management service.
Customers can customize these templates or build policies from scratch using a simple visual policy builder in the AWS Management Console.

claim: A traffic policy is the set of routing rules and does nothing by itself; a policy record associates the traffic policy with a DNS name in a hosted zone you own.
question: What is the difference between a traffic policy and a policy record?

values.display: policy record

evidence.quote: A traffic policy is the set of rules that you define to route end users’ requests to one of your application’s endpoints.
By itself, a traffic policy doesn’t affect how end users are routed to your application because it isn’t yet associated with your application’s DNS name (such as www.example.com).

claim: Traffic Flow is billed per policy record, monthly and prorated for partial months; a traffic policy without a policy record is not charged.
question: How is Traffic Flow billed, and is a traffic policy without a policy record charged?

values.display: billed per policy record

qualifiers.condition: billing is monthly and prorated for partial months

evidence.quote: You are billed per policy record.
Billing is monthly and is prorated for partial months.
We only charge for policy records; there is no charge for creating the traffic policy itself.

claim: One traffic policy can manage several DNS names through extra policy records (each billed) or through CNAME records that point at one policy record, but the CNAME method is not possible at the zone apex, where you must create a policy record.
question: Can one traffic policy manage more than one DNS name, and what is the limit of the CNAME method?

values.display: not possible for records at the zone apex

evidence.quote: Note that this method is not possible for records at the zone apex, such as example.net, example.org, or example.co.uk (without www or another subdomain in front of the domain name).
For records at the zone apex, you must create a policy record using your traffic policy.

claim: Traffic Flow supports all Route 53 DNS routing policies and also supports geoproximity routing with traffic biasing.
question: Which routing types does Traffic Flow support?

values.display: geoproximity based routing with traffic biasing

evidence.quote: In addition to these, Traffic Flow also supports geoproximity based routing with traffic biasing.

claim: In a geoproximity rule you specify either an AWS Region (for AWS resources) or the latitude and longitude of each endpoint, and a user is routed to the geographically closest endpoint.
question: How does a geoproximity rule decide where to send a DNS query?

values.display: latitude and longitude for each endpoint

evidence.quote: When you create a traffic flow policy, you can specify either an AWS region (if you're using AWS resources) or the latitude and longitude for each endpoint.
When an user in Seattle visits your website, geoproximity routing will route the DNS query to the EC2 instances in the US West (Oregon) region because it's closer geographically.

claim: Changing the geoproximity bias value on an endpoint expands or shrinks the area from which traffic is routed to that resource, but bias cannot accurately predict the load factor.
question: What does the geoproximity bias value do, and can it predict load?

values.display: expands or shrinks the area

evidence.quote: Changing the geoproximity bias value on an endpoint either expands or shrinks the area from which Route 53 routes traffic to a resource.

The geoproximity bias can't accurately predict the load factor, though, because a small shift in the size of geographic areas might include or exclude major metropolitan areas that generate large numbers of queries.

claim: As the FAQ is written, bias can be applied only to geoproximity rules in Traffic Flow.
question: Can bias be applied to Traffic Flow rules other than geoproximity?

values.display: bias can only be applied to geoproximity rules

evidence.quote: As of today, bias can only be applied to geoproximity rules.
